title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 81–82
description: British English sound-symbolic vocabulary, animal calls, homophones, homographs and pronunciation contrasts, with original examples and Brazilian Portuguese translations.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow the source teaching pages and exercises; all teaching examples and explanatory notes are independently written. Original exercises, passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Complete teaching pages, illustrations, exercise vocabulary and relevant answer-key entries checked for vocabulary, senses and pronunciation contrasts.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA; homophone sets use shared pronunciations where valid in standard southern British English. Homographs distinguish the relevant spoken forms. Browser speech-synthesis differences are possible.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared against the supplied PDF pages and answer key; curated original examples; structural, ID, source coverage and word-audio/sentence-audio static checks. No app import or browser testing was available.
audit.limitations: No bundled audio, no live app import, no speech-recognition tests and no browser TTS tests. Accent- and voice-dependent pronunciation may vary.

units.title: Unit 81 — Onomatopoeic words
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 168–169 (PDF pages 169–170).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Understand how onomatopoeic vocabulary imitates or evokes real-world sounds.
Recognise animal calls and distinguish sounds made by animals, people and objects.
Use words beginning with gr-, cl-, sp- and wh- in their natural contexts.
Use vivid words ending in -ash and recognise their meanings and verb patterns.

items.example: Buzz is an onomatopoeic word because its sound resembles a noise.
items.note: An onomatopoeic word imitates or suggests the sound it describes.

items.example: The cows began to moo when the farmer arrived.
items.note: The characteristic low call of a cow.

items.example: Our cat likes to meow outside the kitchen door.
items.note: Also written miaow, especially in British English.

items.example: The kitten started to purr as soon as I stroked it.
items.note: A quiet vibrating sound that cats often make when content.

items.example: We heard a lion roar somewhere beyond the fence.
items.note: A loud, deep animal call; can also describe a powerful human or mechanical sound.

items.example: Several bees continued to buzz around the flowers.
items.note: The continuous humming sound of insects or some machines.

items.example: A small bird began to tweet outside the window.
items.note: A short high-pitched bird sound; also a social-media verb in another context.

items.example: He let out a groan when he tried to lift the heavy box.
items.note: A long, low sound expressing pain, frustration or disappointment.

items.example: The passengers began to grumble about the lengthy delay.
items.note: To complain quietly or bad-temperedly; often grumble about something.

items.example: I get grumpy when I have not slept enough.
items.note: Describes someone who is easily annoyed and bad-tempered.

items.example: The dog began to growl when a stranger approached.
items.note: A deep warning sound; people can also growl a reply.

items.example: Click the blue button to save your changes.
items.note: A short, sharp sound; in computing, to press a mouse button or screen control.

items.example: The empty metal bucket fell with a loud clang.
items.note: A sharp, loud ringing noise, usually from metal objects.

items.pt: som ritmado dos cascos de cavalo
items.example: We could hear the clip-clop of hooves on the stone road.
items.note: Imitates the repeated sound of a horse walking on a hard surface.

items.example: The children loved to splash water in the paddling pool.
items.note: To make liquid scatter or fall in drops.

items.example: Please do not spit chewing gum onto the pavement.
items.note: Irregular verb: spit, spat, spat in standard British English.

items.example: He had to spit out the food because it was far too hot.
items.note: A phrasal verb meaning to force something out of the mouth.

items.example: Spray a little water onto the leaves each morning.
items.note: To distribute liquid as a fine mist of small drops.

items.example: She left her hairspray in the bathroom cabinet.
items.note: A product sprayed onto hair to keep a hairstyle in place.

items.example: Sprinkle some chopped herbs over the vegetables.
items.note: Usually sprinkle something on or over food; also used for water.

items.example: Water began to spurt from a damaged pipe.
items.note: Liquid suddenly comes out in a forceful burst; often spurt from or out of.

items.example: She began to whistle a cheerful tune on her walk home.
items.note: A high-pitched sound produced by forcing air through a small opening.

items.pt: passar zunindo; fazer um zumbido veloz
items.example: A tiny drone whizzed past the garden.
items.note: To move quickly with a humming or rushing sound.

items.example: After running upstairs, he stopped to wheeze and catch his breath.
items.note: To breathe noisily with a whistling sound.

items.example: The falling shelf managed to smash two glass jars.
items.note: To break something violently, often into pieces.

items.example: I had to dash to the station to catch the train.
items.note: To run or move quickly, usually because you are in a hurry.

items.example: The car began to skid and crash into the barrier.
items.note: A violent collision, often making a loud noise.

items.pt: acidente de carro; colisão de carro
items.example: Nobody was injured in the car crash.
items.note: A common noun phrase for a collision involving a car.

items.example: Be careful not to bash your knee against the table.
items.note: To hit something hard, often causing damage.

items.example: Mash the boiled potatoes with a fork.
items.note: To crush cooked food until it becomes soft.

items.example: We served the stew with mashed potato.
items.note: Mashed is the past participle of mash; in British English, mashed potato is a usual mass-noun phrase.

items.example: She had a deep gash on her leg after the fall.
items.note: A long, deep cut, especially in the skin.

items.example: The hens began to cluck as we entered the barn.
items.note: The repeated short sound made by a hen.

items.example: A lost lamb started to bleat loudly in the field.
items.note: The characteristic call of a sheep or goat.

items.example: The snake began to hiss when it felt threatened.
items.note: A long sharp /s/-like sound, also produced by escaping air.

sectionsChecked: B: Letters, sounds and their associations (gr-, cl-, sp-, wh-, -ash)

units.title: Unit 82 — Homophones and homographs
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 170–171 (PDF pages 171–172).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Recognise common British English homophones and choose spellings according to meaning and grammar.
Distinguish homographs with different pronunciations, including present/past verb forms and noun/verb contrasts.
Avoid common errors such as weather versus whether and its versus it’s.
Recognise wordplay based on similar pronunciation or multiple meanings.

items.example: Flour and flower are a familiar pair of homophones.
items.note: Homophones sound alike but differ in spelling and meaning.

items.example: The word lead is a homograph with two pronunciations.
items.note: Homographs share their written form but differ in meaning and sometimes pronunciation.

items.example: The air in the laboratory felt unusually dry.
items.note: Sounds like heir but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The heir was expected to inherit the family estate.
items.note: Sounds like air but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Read the instructions aloud before the activity.
items.note: Sounds like allowed but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Visitors are not allowed into the restricted area.
items.note: Sounds like aloud but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Please take a short break before the next session.
items.note: Sounds like brake but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Press the brake gently on a wet road.
items.note: Sounds like break but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The train fare is cheaper when you book early.
items.note: Sounds like fair but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: That seems like a fair way to divide the costs.
items.note: Sounds like fare but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Unexpected criticism did not faze her.
items.note: Sounds like phase but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The project entered its final testing phase.
items.note: Sounds like faze but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: She stayed at home because she had the flu.
items.note: Sounds like flew but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: They flew to Edinburgh on Friday.
items.note: Sounds like flu but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Grate a little cheese over the hot pasta.
items.note: Sounds like great but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: He made great progress during the course.
items.note: Sounds like grate but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The whole audience gave a groan of disappointment.
items.note: Sounds like grown but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The children have grown much taller this year.
items.note: Sounds like groan but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: My voice sounded hoarse after the concert.
items.note: Sounds like horse but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The horse stopped beside the wooden gate.
items.note: Sounds like hoarse but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.pt: seu; sua; dele; dela (possessivo de coisa ou animal)
items.example: The company updated its security policy.
items.note: Sounds like it’s but has a different meaning or spelling. A possessive determiner; unlike it’s, it has no apostrophe.

items.pt: é; está; é que (contração de it is ou it has)
items.example: It’s been a busy week for our team.
items.note: Sounds like its but has a different meaning or spelling. The apostrophe means it is or it has; its has no apostrophe.

items.example: The hen lays an egg almost every day.
items.note: Sounds like laze but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.pt: ficar à toa; relaxar sem fazer nada
items.example: We plan to laze by the pool all afternoon.
items.note: Sounds like lays but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The package arrived with the morning mail.
items.note: Sounds like male but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The male bird has brighter feathers.
items.note: Sounds like mail but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: We rarely eat meat during the week.
items.note: Sounds like meet but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: We should meet near the library entrance.
items.note: Sounds like meat but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The freshly mown lawn looked tidy.
items.note: Sounds like moan but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: He tends to moan about the traffic.
items.note: Sounds like mown but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Our train leaves in ten minutes.
items.note: Sounds like hour but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The lecture lasted just over an hour.
items.note: Sounds like our but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: I bought a new pair of gloves.
items.note: Sounds like pear, pare but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: She sliced a ripe pear for breakfast.
items.note: Sounds like pair, pare but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Pare the fruit carefully with a small knife.
items.note: Sounds like pair, pear but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Her face went pale when she heard the news.
items.note: Sounds like pail but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The child filled a pail with sand.
items.note: Sounds like pale but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The builder replaced a cracked window pane.
items.note: Sounds like pain but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: He felt a sharp pain in his shoulder.
items.note: Sounds like pane but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: A peal of bells rang out across the village.
items.note: Sounds like peel but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Keep the orange peel for the cake.
items.note: Sounds like peal but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: There is a quiet place to study upstairs.
items.note: Sounds like plaice but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: We ordered grilled plaice for dinner.
items.note: Sounds like place but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: You need to practise speaking every day.
items.note: Sounds like practice but has a different meaning or spelling. In British English, practise is the verb; practice is the noun.

items.example: Regular practice will improve your pronunciation.
items.note: Sounds like practise but has a different meaning or spelling. In British English, practice is the noun; practise is the verb.

items.example: Some people pray before an important decision.
items.note: Sounds like prey but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The owl caught its prey in the field.
items.note: Sounds like pray but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The company plans to raise salaries next year.
items.note: Sounds like rays but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The sun’s rays reached the valley floor.
items.note: Sounds like raise but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: I read technical articles every morning.
items.note: Sounds like reed but has a different meaning or spelling. Here read is the present-tense form /riːd/, not the past-tense form /red/.

items.example: A broken reed made the clarinet difficult to play.
items.note: Sounds like read but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: She loosened the rein to let the horse walk.
items.note: Sounds like rain, reign but has a different meaning or spelling. Reins are usually mentioned in the plural when holding both.

items.example: Heavy rain delayed the match.
items.note: Sounds like rein, reign but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The queen’s reign lasted several decades.
items.note: Sounds like rein, rain but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: You gave the right answer to the question.
items.note: Sounds like rite, write but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The ceremony included an ancient rite.
items.note: Sounds like right, write but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Please write your name at the top of the form.
items.note: Sounds like right, rite but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The shop announced a winter sale.
items.note: Sounds like sail but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: A red sail appeared on the horizon.
items.note: Sounds like sale but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The film opens with a dramatic scene.
items.note: Sounds like seen but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: I have seen that documentary before.
items.note: Sounds like scene but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The northern lights were an amazing sight.
items.note: Sounds like site but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The new factory site is near the motorway.
items.note: Sounds like sight but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: It was raining, so we stayed indoors.
items.note: Sounds like sew but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: She can sew a button onto a shirt.
items.note: Sounds like so but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: There was a small hole in the sole of my shoe.
items.note: Sounds like soul but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The song seemed to speak to her soul.
items.note: Sounds like sole but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Would you like some fresh coffee?
items.note: Sounds like sum but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The sum of the two figures is correct.
items.note: Sounds like some but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: He ordered a steak with roasted vegetables.
items.note: Sounds like stake but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The investor bought a small stake in the firm.
items.note: Sounds like steak but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Would you prefer tea or coffee?
items.note: Sounds like tee but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: She placed the golf ball on the tee.
items.note: Sounds like tea but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Put the tools over there, please.
items.note: Sounds like their, they’re but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The students handed in their essays.
items.note: Sounds like there, they’re but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.pt: eles são; eles estão (contração de they are)
items.example: They’re working on a new design.
items.note: Sounds like there, their but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: We walked through the tunnel.
items.note: Sounds like threw but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: He threw the keys onto the table.
items.note: Sounds like through but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Long journeys can tire even experienced drivers.
items.note: Sounds like tyre but has a different meaning or spelling. Tyre, not tire, is the usual British spelling for a vehicle wheel covering.

items.example: The mechanic replaced the damaged front tyre.
items.note: Sounds like tire but has a different meaning or spelling. Tyre is the standard British spelling for a vehicle wheel covering.

items.example: I hurt my big toe while playing football.
items.note: Sounds like tow but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: A truck arrived to tow the broken-down car.
items.note: Sounds like toe but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The coat fitted neatly around her waist.
items.note: Sounds like waste but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Leaving the lights on all day is a waste of energy.
items.note: Sounds like waist but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: Please wait until the equipment has cooled.
items.note: Sounds like weight but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The maximum weight is printed on the label.
items.note: Sounds like wait but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The signal was too weak to detect reliably.
items.note: Sounds like week but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: I have an interview next week.
items.note: Sounds like weak but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The weather improved just before lunch.
items.note: Sounds like whether but has a different meaning or spelling. Weather describes atmospheric conditions, not a choice.

items.example: I cannot decide whether to apply for the course.
items.note: Sounds like weather but has a different meaning or spelling. Whether introduces a choice or uncertainty, not atmospheric conditions.

items.example: Stop whining about the small delay.
items.note: Sounds like wine but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: They served a glass of wine with dinner.
items.note: Sounds like whine but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: I would like to ask one more question.
items.note: Sounds like wood but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: The desk is made from recycled wood.
items.note: Sounds like would but has a different meaning or spelling.

items.example: We sat in the back row of the theatre.
items.note: Noun: a line of people or seats; contrasts with row /raʊ/ meaning argument.

items.example: The neighbours had a row about the noise.
items.note: British English noun for an argument; contrasts with row /rəʊ/ meaning line.

items.example: They live near the coast.
items.note: Verb meaning reside or remain alive; pronounced /lɪv/.

items.example: The interview will be broadcast live tonight.
items.note: Adjective or adverb describing a real-time performance or transmission.

items.example: I usually read for half an hour before bed.
items.note: Present form or infinitive; contrasts with the identical spelling of past read /red/.

items.example: Last weekend I read the entire report.
items.note: Past simple or past participle of read, pronounced /red/.

items.example: Experienced engineers lead the project team.
items.note: Verb to guide; also a noun pronounced /liːd/ in lead singer.

items.example: Old paint sometimes contains lead.
items.note: Noun for the chemical element, pronounced /led/.

items.example: A strong wind shook the windows.
items.note: Noun for moving air; contrasts with verb wind /waɪnd/.

items.example: Wind the cable around the spool carefully.
items.note: Verb meaning twist or wrap; irregular wind, wound, wound.

items.example: He wound the cable around the reel yesterday.
items.note: Past tense of wind /waɪnd/ meaning wrap; not the noun wound /wuːnd/.

items.example: The nurse cleaned the wound and covered it.
items.note: Noun for an injury to the body; contrasts with wound /waʊnd/.

items.example: This device has several practical uses, but its main use is monitoring.
items.note: Noun; the final consonant is /s/, unlike the verb use /juːz/.

items.example: We use a digital sensor for this measurement.
items.note: Verb; the final consonant is voiced /z/.

items.example: They bought a small house near the station.
items.note: Noun for a dwelling; the final consonant is /s/.

items.example: The new facility will house several research groups.
items.note: Verb meaning provide space or accommodation; the final consonant is /z/.

items.example: The sow was resting beside her piglets.
items.note: Noun for an adult female pig; pronounced /saʊ/.

items.example: Farmers sow wheat in early autumn.
items.note: Verb for putting seeds in the ground; pronounced /səʊ/.

items.example: Bathing a baby requires care and patience.
items.note: From bath /bɑːθ/ as a verb /bɑːð/ in British English; contrasts with bathing /ˈbeɪðɪŋ/.

items.pt: banho de mar; natação em área de banho
items.example: Bathing is prohibited in the lake during winter.
items.note: From bathe /beɪð/, used especially for swimming or bathing in open water.

items.example: The chef served smoked fish roe with toast.
items.note: Homophone of row /rəʊ/ in the sense of a line; roe means fish eggs.

items.example: He wore a blue bow tie to the ceremony.
items.note: As a noun for a decorative knot, bow rhymes with go; contrasts with bow /baʊ/.

items.example: The musician took a bow at the end of the concert.
items.note: A gesture of bending forward; pronounced /baʊ/, unlike bow /bəʊ/ on a tie.

items.example: She put on a woolly jumper before going outside.
items.note: In British English, jumper commonly means a knitted sweater.

items.example: The athlete was an excellent high jumper.
items.note: A jumper can also mean someone or something that jumps.

items.example: An icy draught came through the gap under the door.
items.note: British spelling draught; American draft for a current of air.

items.example: We played draughts after dinner.
items.note: British English game name; usually checkers in American English.

items.example: The child began to draw a picture of the garden.
items.note: Draw can mean make lines or a picture.

items.example: Please draw the curtains before the film begins.
items.note: The verb draw here means pull; usually close curtains, though context can indicate opening them.

items.example: The date of the exam is printed on the notice.
items.note: A day, month and year or a particular day.

items.example: She added chopped dates to the cake mixture.
items.note: An edible sweet fruit of the date palm.

items.example: They went on their first date last Saturday.
items.note: A social or romantic meeting arranged for a particular time.

items.example: The drummer began to beat the drum in time with the music.
items.note: Beat can mean strike repeatedly.

items.example: That performance will take some beating.
items.note: Idiom meaning to be hard to improve on; also used as take a lot of beating.
